text: A pipeline is a logical grouping of activities that together perform one single unit of work. An activity can take zero or more input datasets and produce one or more output datasets — Chapter 2 built the connections at the bottom of this chain, and this entire chapter builds everything above it.

The real benefit here: you manage, deploy, and schedule activities as one set, instead of one at a time. A pipeline that ingests log data and then kicks off a transformation is genuinely one thing to trigger, monitor, and retry — not two or three separate things you'd otherwise have to coordinate entirely by hand.
In the Author hub, select the plus icon, choose Pipeline, then Pipeline again from the submenu. That opens the pipeline editor itself, ready for real work.

Four panes worth knowing by name, since every remaining lesson in this chapter genuinely lives inside them. Activities, listing every type available to drag in. The canvas, where they land and get wired together. A configuration pane for parameters, variables, and settings. And a properties pane for the pipeline's own name and description.

Every single activity Data Factory supports falls into exactly one of three real categories. Data movement copies data from a source to a sink. Data transformation processes or reshapes it using a compute engine. And control manages the flow of the pipeline itself, not the data moving through it.

A pipeline supports a default soft limit of 120 activities, generous for nearly any real pipeline you'll actually build. Next: the Copy activity, hands-on — the one activity nearly every real pipeline includes somewhere.
